name: Dickinsonia
description: A soft-bodied, oval organism with a ribbed body made of repeated segments. Dickinsonia lived on the seafloor long before animals with hard shells became common. Its fossils are among the most recognizable finds from the Ediacaran hills of South Australia.
discovery: Geologist Reginald C. Sprigg found the Ediacaran fossil beds in 1946 and introduced the name Dickinsonia in 1947.

name: Burgessomedusa
description: A large, bell-shaped jellyfish from the Cambrian seas, with tentacles that may have helped it catch prey. Its exceptionally preserved fossils show that swimming medusae were already part of ocean ecosystems more than 500 million years ago.
discovery: Most of the 182 known fossils were collected from Raymond Quarry in the late 1980s and 1990s under the supervision of Royal Ontario Museum paleontologist Desmond Collins. Joseph Moysiuk, Jean-Bernard Caron, and Justin Moon formally described the species in 2023.
imageCredit: Justin Moon, Jean-Bernard Caron and Joseph Moysiuk · CC BY 4.0
sourceLabel: Proceedings of the Royal Society B paper

name: Atlantic horseshoe crab
age: Relatives are known from fossils over 450 million years old
description: Despite its name, this animal is more closely related to spiders than to true crabs. The Atlantic horseshoe crab is a living species in a much older lineage, with a domed shell, long tail spine, and a vital role in coastal ecosystems.
discovery: Carl Linnaeus formally described the living Atlantic species in 1758. That is its scientific description date, not the discovery date of the much older horseshoe-crab lineage.
imageAlt: Atlantic horseshoe crab on a beach

name: Anomalocaris
description: One of the largest predators in Cambrian seas, Anomalocaris swam using flexible side flaps and seized prey with spiny frontal appendages. Its circular mouth and remarkable size made it one of the most distinctive animals of the Burgess Shale ecosystem.
discovery: Canadian geologist Joseph Frederick Whiteaves described the first isolated Anomalocaris fossil in 1892. For decades, different parts of the animal were mistaken for separate creatures.

name: Hallucigenia
description: This tiny, worm-like animal had a row of spines along its back and pairs of soft legs underneath. Its unusual shape puzzled scientists for decades; careful study of Burgess Shale fossils eventually helped resolve which side was up and where its head belonged.
discovery: Charles Doolittle Walcott collected the fossils in 1911. Simon Conway Morris re-examined them and introduced the name Hallucigenia in 1977.

name: Opabinia
description: Opabinia had five eyes and a flexible, clawed proboscis that it may have used to handle food. Known from the Burgess Shale, this small marine animal became famous for its unusual body plan and the challenges it posed to early attempts at classification.
discovery: Charles Doolittle Walcott collected the Burgess Shale fossils and formally described Opabinia in 1912. Harry Whittington's detailed redescription in 1975 revealed how unusual its anatomy was.

name: Tiktaalik
description: Tiktaalik combined fish features, including scales and fins, with a flattened skull, a flexible neck, and strong fin bones capable of supporting its body in shallow water. Its anatomy offers a glimpse of adaptations near the evolutionary transition between fish and the earliest land vertebrates.
discovery: A research team led by Neil Shubin, Edward Daeschler, and Farish Jenkins discovered the fossils on Ellesmere Island in 2004. The species was formally described in 2006.
imageAlt: Scientific reconstruction of Tiktaalik in shallow water
imageCredit: Zina Deretsky / National Science Foundation · Public domain

name: Archaeopteryx
description: Archaeopteryx lived in what is now southern Germany and is known from finely preserved fossils that include clear feather impressions. It had a mix of bird-like and dinosaur-like traits, making it an important fossil for studying the early evolution of birds.
discovery: The first widely recognized specimen was found near Solnhofen, Germany, in 1861; the quarry worker who found it is not known. Hermann von Meyer named and described Archaeopteryx that year.
imageAlt: Berlin specimen of the Archaeopteryx fossil

name: Tyrannosaurus rex
description: Tyrannosaurus rex was a large carnivorous dinosaur with powerful jaws, sharp teeth, and a strong sense of smell. It lived in western North America near the end of the Cretaceous Period, and many discoveries have helped researchers study its growth and biology.
discovery: Barnum Brown unearthed the first recognized T. rex skeleton in Montana in 1902. Henry Fairfield Osborn formally named and described Tyrannosaurus rex in 1905.
